title: Homeschooling Is More Normal Than You Think
author: Mere Orthodoxy
summary: This is a review of Dixie Dillon Lane's Skipping School: A History of American Homeschooling, framed by the reviewer's own day homeschooling four children. The review's central argument is that homeschooling isn't the historical outlier it's often taken to be — it's one recurring expression of a much older American pattern of parental authority over children's formation, traceable through Pierce v. Society of Sisters back to colonial-era community schooling norms. Using Lane's case studies (a 1953 Los Angeles homeschooling mother interrogated about Communism; a second-generation homeschooler diagnosed with ADHD only in college; an African-American ministry family homeschooling to shield their kids from neighborhood violence while still serving their block), the reviewer argues homeschooling families today are 'postinstitutional' rather than simply anti-institutional. The piece's deepest claim is about family sovereignty: the family, not the school or the state, is the more fundamental institution, and homeschooling read historically is one continuous thread of resistance to treating children as 'creatures of the state.' It closes by tying homeschooling's growth to a broader craving for 'thickened,' multigenerational community that institutional schooling structurally cannot provide.
points: Frames homeschooling as continuous with an older American tradition of parental primacy in education, dating at least to Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925).
Today's homeschoolers are 'postinstitutional' rather than anti-institutional — many build their own cooperatives, networks, and even classical/Catholic schools.
The 1950s legal gray zone around homeschooling was entangled with Cold War anxiety: not sending your kids to public school could get you accused of being a Communist.
One case study shows a family living in and serving a high-crime neighborhood while homeschooling their own kids to protect them from 'the violent gang mind' without abandoning their neighbors.

quotes: Homeschooling in America today is "the site of a flourishing range of pedagogies, curricula, and experiments in education," reflecting the diversity of Americans.

They didn't send their children to district schools because they didn't want them to grow up with "the violent gang mind." But they would invite the neighbor kids—many from broken homes—over to their house after school hours to give them a safe haven and the experience of a loving home.

Homeschooling matters because by its very nature—in all its non-standardized, messy, unwieldy glory—it is a movement against the professionalization, standardization, and replacement of the human being.
